title.rendered: Love Your Neighbor As Yourself: The Gospel For Today

content.rendered:
A traveler lay half-dead in a ditch on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest passed by. A Levite passed by. Then, unexpectedly, a Samaritan stopped. That story is Jesus’ answer to the question, “Who is my neighbor?”

The Gospel For Today | Monday, September 21, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“And the second, like it, is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”
Mark 12:31 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

A traveler lay half-dead in a ditch on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. He had been beaten, stripped, and robbed. A priest walked by on the other side of the road. A Levite walked by on the other side of the road. Then, unexpectedly, a man from Samaria stopped. In the world of first-century Israel, Samaritans and Jews did not associate. The listeners hearing Jesus tell the story would have expected the Samaritan to walk on faster than the priest. Instead, the Samaritan bandaged the traveler’s wounds, put him on his own donkey, took him to an inn, paid the innkeeper out of his own pocket, and promised to pay any additional cost on his return. Jesus told that story in Luke 10 in response to a lawyer who wanted to narrow the definition of “neighbor” down to something manageable. And when Jesus asked the lawyer which of the three men had been a neighbor to the traveler in the ditch, the lawyer could barely say the word. “The one who showed mercy.”

Yesterday we heard Jesus name the first great commandment. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength. Today He names the second. “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.” The love of God and the love of neighbor are not two separate assignments. They are two sides of the same commandment. The believer who loves God rightly finds themselves loving neighbour naturally. The believer who ignores the neighbour has misunderstood what loving God actually is.

The Passion Translation renders the commandment: “And the second is this: ‘You must love your friend in the same way you love yourself.’ You will never find a greater commandment than these” (Mark 12:31 TPT). The Amplified Bible Classic Edition adds: “The second is like it and is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these” (Mark 12:31 AMPC). Notice the yardstick Jesus places on the loving. As yourself. The way you attend to your own needs. The way you defend your own interests. The way you speak up when you are the one hungry, tired, or overlooked. That kind of care, extended to the person in front of you.

The Good Samaritan story makes the definition of “neighbour” impossible to narrow. It is not the person of your ethnicity, your religion, your class, your neighbourhood, or your political tribe. It is the person in front of you who needs mercy. In the story Jesus told, the neighbour was the last person the audience expected. The despised Samaritan. And the “religious” people who should have known better were the ones who kept walking. Jesus never let His listeners hide behind theology to avoid loving a real human being.

For Gospelbuzz readers today, this is the working command of every day. Wherever you are reading this from, in Lagos or London or Manila or Nairobi or Sao Paulo, there is a neighbour in your life today who needs the mercy God has given you. Someone in the ditch. Someone overlooked. Someone the “religious” people are walking past. Do not walk past them. Cross the road. Bandage the wound. Pay the cost. Love your neighbour as yourself, because in the loving of them, you are loving the God who first loved you.

Prayer

Father, I acknowledge that You have called me to love my neighbour as myself. There is no small print in this commandment. There is no ethnic exception. There is no religious loophole. There is no political filter. The neighbour is the person in front of me who needs mercy. Today I ask You to open my eyes. Show me the ones in the ditch on the road of my ordinary life. Give me the courage to cross the road. Give me the generosity to pay the cost. Let my love for my neighbour be the visible outflow of the love You have already given me in Christ. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

I love my neighbour as myself. The person in front of me who needs mercy is my neighbour. I cross the road. I bandage the wound. I pay the cost. In loving them, I love the God who first loved me.
